summary: RPL normally routes packets hop by hop along a DODAG, which may not be efficient. This document lets the root install routing state to improve paths. It updates RFC 6550, RFC 6553 and RFC 8138.

plainLanguage.summary: RPL is the routing protocol used in networks of small, battery-powered devices. It builds a tree towards a root, so traffic between two devices has to travel up to the root and back down even when the two are close together. This document lets the root install better routes, computed centrally, so packets can travel directly. The root does this with new messages and options that extend RPL.

questions: what is a projected dao in rpl
what is a p-route in rpl
what is a track in rpl
how does the rpl root install routes
subtitle: How a RPL root installs optimised routes in a low-power network, so packets need not climb to the root and back.

tldr.problem: RPL routes every packet along its tree, so two devices that sit close to each other still send their traffic up to the root and back down, which costs hops, latency and energy in a battery-powered network.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines DAO Projection. A path computation element works out a path, and the root installs it as a Projected Route using new Projected DAO messages, either as a Storing Mode segment installed hop by hop or as a Non-Storing Mode protection path source-routed by the track ingress.
tldr.outcome: A set of P-Routes can be combined into a Track, signalled as its own RPL Instance with its own routing table. The document updates RFC 6550, RFC 6553 and RFC 8138 to carry the new messages, options and flags.

today: RFC 9914 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2026. It updates RFC 6550, RFC 6553 and RFC 8138, and it builds on the RPL data plane work in RFC 9008 and on the Reliable and Available Wireless architecture in RFC 9912.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RPL, the Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks, defined in RFC 6550, is a distance vector protocol for networks of small, battery-powered devices. It is anisotropic, which means it behaves differently in each direction: routes down from the root are advertised with multicast DIO messages, and routes up towards the root are advertised with unicast DAO messages.

RPL forms Destination-Oriented Directed Acyclic Graphs (DODAGs). Routers inside a DODAG send traffic up towards the root for the default route and down towards destinations in the domain for more specific routes. The document assumes a pre-existing main Instance, main DODAG and main Root, operated in Non-Storing Mode, and it adds a component called a Path Computation Element (PCE), which may be a central controller or may sit with the main Root.

The PCE computes additional paths between nodes in the main Instance, using the topology the root already holds plus the sibling relationships the document adds. The root then projects those computed paths into the network as Projected Routes, or P-Routes, on behalf of the PCE. A P-Route may be installed in Storing or Non-Storing Mode, so the mode of a P-Route can differ from the mode of the main Instance. A P-Route can stand alone as a segment that shortens the Source Routing Header, act as a protection path, or be combined with other P-Routes into a larger structure called a Track, which is signalled as a separate RPL Instance with its own routing table.
sections.plainLanguage: RPL builds a tree towards a root, and two nearby devices still send their traffic up to the root and back down. This document lets a central planner work out a better path and lets the root install it, so packets can travel directly. The root uses new messages and options that extend RPL.

sections.title: Projected Routes, Tracks and Segments
sections.content:
The document defines its own terms. A Projected Route (P-Route) is a RPL route computed remotely by a PCE and installed and maintained by a RPL Root on behalf of that PCE. A Projected DAO (P-DAO) is the DAO message used to install one.

A Track is a networking graph that can be followed to transport packets with equivalent treatment. It is not necessarily linear: it may hold several paths that fork and rejoin, which lets it carry redundant copies of a packet. The document builds Tracks that are DODAGs oriented towards a Track ingress, and the forward direction for packets runs from that ingress to one of possibly several egress nodes. A Track is normally a collection of parallel loose source-routed sequences of nodes running from ingress to egress, each one forming a protection path.

Two kinds of piece make up a Track. A segment is a serial path with a strict sequence of nodes, typically installed by the root with Storing Mode P-DAO messages, so that every node along it holds a route. A protection path is installed with a Non-Storing Mode P-DAO and keeps its state only at the Track ingress, which source-routes the packet. A Complex Track is a Track that can be traversed by more than one path.
sections.plainLanguage: A projected route is a route the root installs on behalf of a central planner. A track is a set of ways to carry a packet from one node to another, and it can offer more than one path, so a failure does not stop the traffic. A track is built from segments, where every node keeps a route, and protection paths, where only the entry node keeps state and tells the packet where to go.

sections.title: Why RPL Routes Are Stretched
sections.content:
RPL optimises point-to-multipoint paths from the root and multipoint-to-point paths towards it, but point-to-point traffic has to follow the same DODAG. In Non-Storing Mode a packet travels all the way up to the root, and the root then source-routes it back down, even when the destination is close to the source. In Storing Mode the packet travels up to a common parent and then down again. The document calls this elongated path stretched, and notes that the stretch adds delay and extra chances of loss, both of which are costly in a constrained network.

The stretch also costs at the root. In Non-Storing Mode the root must add a Source Routing Header to every downward packet, and that header grows with the depth of the network, which matters for a network of street lights strung along a road. A limited amount of well-targeted routing state in selected routers would let the source routing be loose instead of strict and would shrink the header carried in every packet.

The document therefore asks the root to install additional routes inside the main DODAG, to reduce the stretch of some point-to-point routes and to hold the paths within a Service Level Objective in terms of latency or reliability. It contrasts this with RFC 6997, which discovers optimised point-to-point routes in a distributed way, and it notes that the routing state has to be placed where it does the most good, which is a decision that needs global knowledge of the system, the kind of knowledge the root or an associated PCE may hold.
sections.plainLanguage: Two devices that are close together still send their traffic to the root and back, so every packet takes more hops than it needs and carries a longer list of directions. The fix is to let the root install a few extra routes in the right places, so packets can take the direct path and the list of directions in each packet gets shorter.

sections.title: Two Orders That Prevent Loops
sections.content:
Routing in a multi-topology domain can create loops unless strict rules are applied, and the document defines two such orders.

The first order relates to the forwarding method and to the origin of the information used to pick the next hop. The possible methods are: a direct next hop; an indirect neighbour through a common neighbour; a segment; and a nested Track. They are strictly ordered in that way. A method may use any of the lower-order ones but never a higher-order one, so a router forwarding a packet along a segment may use direct or indirect neighbours but may not use a Track. The lower-order methods also take precedence, so a direct neighbour is always preferred over an indirect one or over a segment in the current RPL Instance.

The second order is between RPL Instances, and it is partial. An administrator defines a DODAG of underlay RPL Instances with the main Instance at the root. An Instance may use another Instance as an underlay only if that other Instance is one of its descendants in that graph. Supporting this is REQUIRED between a Track Instance and the main Instance, and OPTIONAL for nested Tracks. When no such graph is provided, nodes consider by default that all Track Instances are children of the main Instance and do not validate the order for nested Tracks, trusting the PCE. A packet forwarded along the main Instance may then be encapsulated into any Track, but a packet forwarded along a Track MUST NOT be forwarded along the default route of the main Instance, because that would leave the end-to-end path uncontrolled.
sections.plainLanguage: Running several routing topologies in one network can send a packet in circles, so the document sets two rules. The first says which way of forwarding to use first: a direct neighbour, then a neighbour of a neighbour, then a segment, and only then another track. The second says which topology may be layered under which, so a packet that came out of a track is never sent back up the main tree.

sections.title: New and Amended RPL Messages
sections.content:
The document amends the DAO message to create the P-DAO. The DAO Base Object gains a TrackID field, holding the Local or Global RPLInstanceID of the DODAG that serves as the Track, and a 1-bit 'P' flag in bit position 2 of the Flags field, which the root sets to 1 in a P-DAO and to 0 otherwise. A 'D' flag signals that the DODAGID field is present, and that field carries the IPv6 address of the Track ingress, which is the address used to source encapsulated packets. The root MUST source the P-DAO with the address that serves as the DODAGID of the main DODAG, and a receiver MUST NOT accept a P-DAO that was not sent by the root of its DODAG, ignoring such a message silently.

Two new control message options carry the routes. The Via Information Option (VIO) is the multi-hop alternative to the Transit Information Option. One VIO is the stateful Storing Mode VIO, which installs a strict hop-by-hop P-Route called a segment; the other is the Non-Storing Mode VIO, which installs a loose source-routed P-Route called a protection path at the Track ingress. A P-DAO carries one or more RPL Target Options naming the destinations, followed by exactly one VIO listing the nodes to follow. The Sibling Information Option (SIO) lets a node advertise candidate neighbours to the root, which the root can then use when building P-Routes.

Two flags are added elsewhere. A new 'P' flag in the RPL Packet Information marks a packet that is being forwarded along a P-Route, and it is not mutable en route. A new 'D' flag, Projected Routes Support, in the RPL DODAG Configuration option tells nodes that the root will install requested Tracks; a legacy parent propagates it unchanged, so it reaches every node in the DODAG. For compressed headers, the document extends RFC 8138 with a P-RPI-6LoRH, which IANA has given the value 8 in both the Elective and the Critical registries.

Two new control messages complete the set. A node that wants a Track sends a P-DAO-REQ to the root, with RPL Control Code 0x09. It names the desired TrackID, carries the requested lifetime in Lifetime Units and an 8-bit wrapping sequence number that the root echoes back. The 'K' flag asks for an acknowledgment and the 'R' flag asks for a Complex Track that offers redundancy. A requested lifetime of 255 means infinity; a requested lifetime of 0 means the Track must be destroyed, for example when the application that wanted it ends. The root answers with a PDR-ACK, RPL Control Code 0x0A, giving the granted Track Lifetime, the echoed sequence number and a status. A status value of 0 with the 'E' flag clear means unqualified acceptance. When the 'E' flag is set the status is a rejection: a 'Transient Failure' status means the request may be retried after a reasonable time, and any other negative status means a permanent error that must be abandoned until something is fixed at the application layer or by network management. If the root cannot maintain the expected service level, it tears the Track down and reports it asynchronously with a PDR-ACK whose Track Lifetime is 0.
sections.plainLanguage: The root tells the network about a new route with a Projected DAO, a DAO message with a new flag and a new field that names the track. The route itself is carried in a new option that lists the nodes to follow, in one of two forms: one that makes every node along the path keep a route, and one that keeps the state at the entry node only. A node asks for a track with a small request message, and the root answers with another that says whether the track was built and for how long it will last.

sections.title: Installing, Maintaining and Tearing Down a Track
sections.content:
The root installs a Track as a collection of P-Routes, one message per segment or protection path. In Storing Mode the root sends the P-DAO to the last node on the path, the segment egress, and the message travels back along the segment, so every node installs a route towards the Targets except the egress, which is expected to reach them already. A node that cannot store the routes rejects the P-DAO with the status 'Out of Resources', and a node that cannot reach its predecessor rejects it with 'Predecessor Unreachable'. In Non-Storing Mode the root sends the P-DAO to the Track ingress, which encapsulates packets with a Routing Header built from the list in the option.

Order matters. A segment must be installed before the protection path that uses it, and stitched segments must be installed from the last to the first, so that a loose hop is always reachable when the path that needs it is installed.

To change a segment, the root sends the new section to the second node of the change, and the message propagates back to the first. The new section is installed from its last node to the first, so every node downstream has already installed its new state before an upstream node switches over. The old section is torn down afterwards, once in-flight packets have drained. A protection path is replaced by installing the new one first and switching over before removing the old, because dropping a Track first would send its traffic back through the root, raising latency and possibly creating a loop in a stitched Track. A P-DAO with a lifetime of 0 tears state down rather than refreshing it, and a Track is torn down by tearing down its segments and protection paths one by one.

When forwarding, a router prefers, in order: self-delivery or Routing Header handling; a direct neighbour; an indirect neighbour through a common neighbour; a route along a segment of the same Track; and finally injection into another Track. A packet that has just come out of a Track is never routed along the default route of the main DODAG, and the node that drops such a packet sends an ICMPv6 error to the root with the new code 'Error in P-Route' so that the root can repair the broken piece.
sections.plainLanguage: Installing a route is done from the far end back, so that when a node switches to the new path, every node after it has already switched. Changing a route works the same way: the new part is put in place first, the old part is removed later so that packets already in flight still arrive. When a router cannot forward a packet on a track, it drops the packet and tells the root, which then repairs the broken section.

sections.title: Profiles and Mixed Networks
sections.content:
The document defines ten profiles, numbered 0 to 9, so that an implementation can take only the part of it that is needed. Profiles 0 and 1 are REQUIRED by all implementations used in constrained networks. Profile 0 is the legacy support of RPL Non-Storing Mode, with routing northwards and strict source routing southwards; it is the prerequisite for all the other profiles. Profile 1 adds Storing Mode P-Route segments along the main DODAG, which balances the size of the Routing Header in the packets against the amount of state held in the intermediate routers of a Non-Storing Mode DODAG. Profile 2 is RECOMMENDED in a high-speed environment, such as a wired one, and uses Non-Storing Mode P-Route segments along the main DODAG to get the same header saving at the cost of an encapsulation. Profiles 3 and above use Local RPL Instances to build arbitrary Tracks rooted at the Track ingress, using the namespace of the Track ingress for the TrackID.

The document can run in a mixed network where some nodes support it and some do not, with one restriction: every node that needs to process a P-DAO must support this specification. How the root learns the capabilities of a node is out of scope. Because a requester may not know whether a Track can effectively be constructed, or whether enough nodes along the preferred path are upgraded, the document suggests setting the 'D' flag in the DIO only when the conditions for success are in place, in particular when all the nodes that could be on the path of the Tracks are upgraded.
sections.plainLanguage: The document offers ten profiles, from the plain legacy behaviour of RPL up to full multi-topology tracks, so a small device can implement only what it needs. Only the first two are required. A network can mix upgraded and old nodes, but every node that has to handle a new message has to be upgraded, so the root should only advertise that tracks are available once that is true.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Every node in a constrained network is RPL-aware and can inject any RPL-based attack. This document uses messages that already exist in RPL, with optional secured versions, so whatever security is deployed for the network also applies to the flows it adds.

The document points out that the nodes depend on the RPL Root and on the RPL-Aware Nodes for their operation, so a trust model is needed to make sure the right devices hold those roles, which is what stops sinkhole attacks. That model could rest on secure joining and link-layer security, as RFC 8505 requires, and the Security Considerations of RFC 6550 and RFC 7416 apply here as well. In particular, link-layer security is needed to prevent a denial-of-service attack in which a rogue router floods the network with forged P-DAO messages and uses up the storage of the routers it attacks.

The document also sets out who may send what: the root MAY generate P-DAO messages but other nodes MUST NOT, and P-DAO-REQ messages MUST be sent to the root. It expects the communication with the root to be authenticated without enforcing a method. The validation of the Via Information Option, which avoids a node appearing twice and so prevents basic loops, is described as a minimal protection: an attacker able to inject P-DAOs can reroute any traffic and rapidly use up critical resources such as spectrum and battery.
sections.plainLanguage: The new messages travel over the same secured versions of RPL messages as the rest of the network, so the security a network already has covers them. The document insists on link-layer security, because a rogue router that floods the network with forged route messages can fill up the storage of the routers it targets. It also says the root is the only node allowed to send these route messages.

viz.caption: TWO WAYS TO INSTALL A PROJECTED ROUTE

cells: Every router on the segment keeps a route towards the Targets.
Only the Track ingress keeps state; it source-routes the packets.
SM-VIO, a strict list of via addresses.
NSM-VIO, a loose list of via addresses.
The P-DAO is passed back hop by hop and each router forwards by its own table.
The ingress encapsulates the packet with a Routing Header built from the list.
Strict continuity, so loops are avoided along the Track.
A via address may not appear twice, or the path would loop.
